card st-heldout-followup-per-ticket  [open]
A red held-out run files one follow-up ticket for each ticket whose steps went red
why: A red run groups its red steps by the ticket they came from, and files one follow-up ticket for each group. Each follow-up builds, fails and stops on its own, so one step that no builder can pass does not hold back the fixes for other tickets.

Each held-out step comes from the brief of one ticket, its source ticket. To keep one hard step from blocking unrelated fixes, a red held-out run groups its red steps by source ticket and files one follow-up ticket per group. Each follow-up cites the cards of its own source ticket and has its own retry cap. A red step that an open follow-up already carries files nothing again.

Example:

- Tickets P and Q are merged. Run R turns step P.2 red, and steps Q.1 and Q.4 red.

1. R files follow-up F1 with step P.2. F1 cites the cards of P.
2. R files follow-up F2 with steps Q.1 and Q.4. F2 cites the cards of Q.
3. F2 stops at its cap. F1 still builds and merges.
4. A later run turns Q.1 red again while F2 is open. F2 already carries Q.1, so nothing is filed.

```
run R:  P.2 ✗   Q.1 ✗   Q.4 ✗
         │        └───┬───┘
         ▼            ▼
        F1 (P)       F2 (Q)      ✗ = red step, (X) = source ticket
```

  -> depends_on      lp-heldout-author  A step author writes the steps from the brief, in parallel with the builder
       why: A step author writes a ticket's steps from that ticket's brief, so each step has one source ticket to group by.
  -> depends_on      st-build-run-cap  A run has no limit on follow-up tickets in v0
       why: A follow-up is a new ticket with its own retry cap, so a group that stops at its cap stops only its own steps.
  -> refines         st-build-run  The merge loop: queue one ticket, merge it on green checks, then run the held-out set
  <- alternative_to  st-heldout-followup-per-ticket:opt0  One follow-up ticket for every red step of the run
  <- alternative_to  st-heldout-followup-per-ticket:opt1  One follow-up ticket for each red step
Options
  st-heldout-followup-per-ticket:opt0  One follow-up ticket for every red step of the run
    why not: It mixes unrelated work. One step that no builder can finish stops the fixes for every other step at the same cap.
  st-heldout-followup-per-ticket:opt1  One follow-up ticket for each red step
    why not: Steps of one ticket often share one cause, so one ticket per step builds the same fix many times and gives merge conflicts between the follow-ups.

#st-heldout-followup-per-ticket is now **decided**. It shows no stale mark.

To pass the contract check at decided, the card needed a kill criterion, so I recorded one:

- **What it measures:** the share of follow-up tickets that hit a merge conflict with another follow-up from the same held-out run. The data comes from the board log.
- **When it fires:** above 30% over 30 days, with at least 10 follow-ups.
- **What it falls back to:** `:opt0`, one follow-up ticket for every red step of the run.

The reason: if follow-ups from different source tickets often conflict at merge, the red steps share one cause, and one combined ticket is better. I chose the numbers 30%, 30 days and 10 follow-ups with no data behind them. Change them if you know better values.

card lp-heldout-mechanics  [decided]
The builder never sees the held-out steps
why: The held-out set only works if the builder cannot see it and the binder cannot make a feature look present.

- One step author per ticket. It runs with no tools; the program stores its answer under .werk/heldout/<run>/. A follow-up ticket gets no step author.
- The binder binds every step of the run in a temporary worktree. If it changes a file outside .werk-heldout/, its whole report is void.
- A binder error files no follow-up. The set runs once more at the end of the run; an error that stays ends the run as heldout and waits for a person.
- One held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. A step that an open follow-up already carries files no second one.
- The red badge stays on the merged ticket after its follow-up goes green.

Known gap: the builder's Read tool can reach .werk/heldout/ by an absolute path. The steps are out of the builder's worktree, not out of its reach.

  -> refines         lp-prod-heldout  The held-out set
  -> depends_on      lp-heldout-author  A step author writes the steps from the brief, in parallel with the builder
       why: The mechanics rest on a separate step author that writes from the brief and never reads the code.
  -> depends_on      lp-heldout-binder  A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
       why: The mechanics enforce the binder rules of this card, so the binder cannot make a feature look present.
  <- depends_on      werk-v0-seams-heldout-folder  The product's browser test run also finds the tests in the binder's folder

Yes. The 4th bullet of #lp-heldout-mechanics says that one held-out run files one follow-up for all newly failed steps. The new card decides one follow-up for each source ticket, and it rejects the one-per-run rule as `:opt0`.

I staged a change on #lp-heldout-mechanics. The change replaces that bullet with a pointer: "A red held-out run files its follow-ups as #st-heldout-followup-per-ticket says." The removed bullet also said that a step an open follow-up already carries files no second follow-up. The new card keeps that rule. I also added a `depends_on` edge from #lp-heldout-mechanics to the new card. Without your accept, the two decided cards still contradict each other.

The current code files one follow-up per run, so it also follows the old rule. It needs a change when you accept.
